title: The route tree: short, medium and deep passes (and why 8 catches can be 303 yards)
html:
Why this lesson now: the Film Room mirror (football-brief, branch film-room) was checked this run. It still holds one logged game file (data/games/gmum7mktl1wy3.json, "Eagles at Bears, Week 3", no snaps logged) and no review files. The backup source (football-film-room, branch "data") couldn't be read: this session's GitHub access covers only the football-brief repo. So there's no new miss of yours to fix, and no snap of yours this connects to yet. It's a new concept tied to tonight's McCarthy prop and Friday's UCLA game.

The big idea: every pass route has a depth.Short routes are safe but gain few yards. Deep routes are risky but gain a lot.Coaches draw all of a receiver's routes from one starting point. That drawing is called the route tree.Passing yards depend more on how deep the catches are than on how many there are.

Labels A–D match the steps below. White = short, blue = medium, yellow = deep. Yellow circles = safeties (defense).

  1. A · Short (0–5 yards): the flat and the slant. The ball comes out fast, before the pass rush gets there.Few yards per catch. J.J. McCarthy threw for 127 yards against the Eagles last week. When deep throws aren't there, yards stay low.
  2. B · Medium (10–15 yards): the out and the dig. An out breaks toward the sideline. A dig (also called an "in") breaks toward the middle.These need about 2.5 seconds of blocking (Lesson 24). They move the chains on 3rd-and-long.
  3. C · Deep (20+ yards): the post, the corner and the go. A post angles to the middle, a corner to the sideline, a go runs straight.UCLA's Ty Dieffenbach went 8 of 16 for 303 yards and 3 TDs at Minnesota. That's 37.9 yards per catch: deep shots to Aidan Mizell (SI).Wednesday, Toledo's Adjatay Dabbs caught 7 passes for 144 yards: 20.6 a catch (theScore).
  4. D · The defense picks what's open. Two deep safeties (Lesson 20) guard the deep routes. So short and medium throws open up underneath.One deep safety leaves one side open for a deep shot. That's the side away from him.
  5. Why it matters for bets: a QB's yards prop depends on route depth.Tonight it's likely to rain at MetLife (64%, AccuWeather). A wet ball usually means fewer deep throws.That helps the board's "J.J. McCarthy: 225+ passing yards" → NO lean.

In your drill: when you log "P", also guess short or deep. Deep clues: long yardage (2nd-and-10, 3rd-and-12), a play-action fake (Lesson 16), only one safety deep. Short clues: 3rd-and-3, a quick snap, two safeties deep.

Real examples to watch: tonight, Commanders at Giants (5:15 p.m. PT, Prime Video): count how many of McCarthy's throws go past 15 yards. Friday, Illinois at UCLA (6:00 p.m. PT, FOX): watch for Dieffenbach's deep shots to Mizell.

Video: search YouTube for "NFL route tree explained," "slant vs. post route," and "Ty Dieffenbach Aidan Mizell touchdown."

Practice it in Football Camp → (Station 5: Plays)

quiz.q: Which of these routes is deep?
quiz.w: The post runs 20+ yards and angles to the middle. Flat and slant are short; the out is medium.

quiz.q: Two safeties play deep. Which throws usually open up?
quiz.w: The safeties guard the deep routes, so the space is underneath them.

quiz.q: A QB goes 8 of 16 for 303 yards. What does that tell you?
o: Mostly deep routes and long catches
quiz.w: That's about 38 yards a catch. Only deep routes do that. It's Ty Dieffenbach at Minnesota.

quiz.q: It's raining hard. What usually happens to passing yards?
o: They go down: fewer deep throws
quiz.w: A wet ball is harder to throw far and to catch. Offenses throw shorter and run more.
